claim: Shprintzen–Goldberg syndrome (SGS) is a multisystemic connective tissue disorder with considerable clinical overlap with Marfan and Loeys–Dietz syndromes.
source: Shprintzen–Goldberg syndrome (SGS) is a multisystemic connective tissue disorder, with considerable clinical overlap with Marfan and Loeys–Dietz syndromes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction, representing established clinical knowledge about SGS.

claim: Marfan and Loeys–Dietz syndromes have commonly been associated with enhanced TGF-β signaling.
source: These syndromes have commonly been associated with enhanced TGF-β signaling.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing view in the literature regarding these syndromes.

claim: In SGS patients, heterozygous point mutations have been mapped to the transcriptional co-repressor SKI.
source: In SGS patients, heterozygous point mutations have been mapped to the transcriptional co-repressor SKI, which is a negative regulator of TGF-β signaling that is rapidly degraded upon ligand stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Carmignac et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012; Schepers et al., 2015) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: SKI is a negative regulator of TGF-β signaling that is rapidly degraded upon ligand stimulation.
source: In SGS patients, heterozygous point mutations have been mapped to the transcriptional co-repressor SKI, which is a negative regulator of TGF-β signaling that is rapidly degraded upon ligand stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work and citations (Le Scolan et al., 2008; Levy et al., 2007; Nagano et al., 2007).

claim: SGS mutations in SKI abolish its binding to phosphorylated SMAD2 and SMAD3.
source: Here we use a combination of structural biology, genome editing, and biochemistry to show that SGS mutations in SKI abolish its binding to phosphorylated SMAD2 and SMAD3.
evidence: This is demonstrated through peptide pulldown assays shown in Figure 4A and 4B, and peptide array in Figure 4E.

claim: SGS mutations result in stabilization of SKI.
source: This results in stabilization of SKI and consequently attenuation of TGF-β responses, both in knockin cells expressing an SGS mutation and in fibroblasts from SGS patients.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B showing SKI protein levels remain stable after Activin treatment in P35S SKI knockin cells, and Figure 7A showing SKI stabilization in patient fibroblasts.

claim: SGS mutations lead to attenuation of TGF-β-induced transcriptional responses.
source: Thus, we reveal that SGS is associated with an attenuation of TGF-β-induced transcriptional responses, and not enhancement, which has important implications for other Marfan-related syndromes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through luciferase reporter assays (Figure 6D) and RNA-seq analysis (Figure 7B, C) showing reduced TGF-β responses in SGS mutant cells.

claim: Common features observed in SGS patients include craniofacial, skeletal, and cardiovascular anomalies.
source: Common features observed in SGS patients include craniofacial, skeletal, and cardiovascular anomalies, ranging from heart valve defects to thoracic aortic aneurysms, all of which are also characteristic of Marfan syndrome (MFS) and Loeys–Dietz syndrome (LDS) (Cook et al., 2015a; Verstraeten et al., 2016; Loeys et al., 2005; Williams et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: SGS patients present with craniosynostosis, intellectual disability, and skeletal muscle hypotonia.
source: In addition, SGS patients present with craniosynostosis, intellectual disability, and skeletal muscle hypotonia (Shprintzen and Goldberg, 1982; Glesby and Pyeritz, 1989; Greally et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: All three syndromes (SGS, MFS, LDS) have been linked to deregulation of the transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) signaling pathway.
source: All three syndromes have been linked to deregulation of the transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) signaling pathway (Cannaerts et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to review literature.

claim: TGF-β family ligands play pleiotropic roles in embryonic development and tissue homeostasis.
source: The TGF-β family of ligands comprises the TGF-βs themselves, Activins, Nodal, bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), and growth differentiation factors (GDFs) and they play pleiotropic roles in embryonic development and tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: TGF-β signaling is deregulated in diverse pathologies.
source: In addition, their signaling is deregulated in diverse pathologies (Miller and Hill, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to review literature.

claim: TGF-β ligands exert their action by binding to type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors at the cell surface.
source: They exert their action by binding to type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors at the cell surface (TGFBR1 and TGFBR2, respectively, for the TGF-βs) (Massagué, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the ligand-bound heterotetrameric receptor complex, the type II receptor phosphorylates and activates the type I receptor.
source: In the resulting ligand-bound heterotetrameric receptor complex, the type II receptor phosphorylates and activates the type I receptor, which in turn phosphorylates the intracellular mediators, the receptor-regulated SMADs (R-SMADs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TGF-β signaling mechanism.

claim: The type I receptor phosphorylates the receptor-regulated SMADs (R-SMADs).
source: In the resulting ligand-bound heterotetrameric receptor complex, the type II receptor phosphorylates and activates the type I receptor, which in turn phosphorylates the intracellular mediators, the receptor-regulated SMADs (R-SMADs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TGF-β signaling mechanism.

claim: Once phosphorylated, R-SMADs (SMAD2 and SMAD3 in the case of TGF-β, Activin, and Nodal) associate with SMAD4.
source: Once phosphorylated, the R-SMADs (SMAD2 and SMAD3 in the case of TGF-β, Activin, and Nodal) associate with the common mediator of the pathway, SMAD4.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TGF-β signaling mechanism.

claim: Heterotrimeric R-SMAD–SMAD4 complexes accumulate in the nucleus where they interact with other transcriptional regulators to activate or repress target gene expression.
source: The resulting heterotrimeric complexes accumulate in the nucleus where they interact with other transcriptional regulators to activate or repress target gene expression (Massagué, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SKI and SKIL act as negative regulators in the TGF-β pathway.
source: Two highly related co-repressors, SKI and SKIL (formerly known as SnoN), act as negative regulators in the pathway (Deheuninck and Luo, 2009; see below).
evidence: This is supported by citation and demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: MFS is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the extracellular matrix protein, Fibrillin 1 (FBN1).
source: MFS is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the extracellular matrix protein, Fibrillin 1 (FBN1) (Dietz et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: FBN1 mutations are thought to increase the bioavailability of TGF-β ligands, as FBN1 binds the latent form of the TGF-βs.
source: These mutations are thought to increase the bioavailability of TGF-β ligands, as FBN1 binds the latent form of the TGF-βs (Neptune et al., 2003; Kaartinen and Warburton, 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: A TGF-β neutralizing antibody significantly improved the lung phenotype in a mouse model of MFS (homozygous Fbn1mgΔ).
source: Supporting the idea that excessive TGF-β signaling contributes to the manifestations of MFS, a TGF-β neutralizing antibody significantly improved the lung phenotype in a mouse model of MFS (homozygous Fbn1mgΔ) (Neptune et al., 2003; Cannaerts et al., 2015) and reduced the occurrence of aortic aneurysms in the Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse model of MFS (Habashi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: A TGF-β neutralizing antibody reduced the occurrence of aortic aneurysms in the Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse model of MFS.
source: Supporting the idea that excessive TGF-β signaling contributes to the manifestations of MFS, a TGF-β neutralizing antibody significantly improved the lung phenotype in a mouse model of MFS (homozygous Fbn1mgΔ) (Neptune et al., 2003; Cannaerts et al., 2015) and reduced the occurrence of aortic aneurysms in the Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse model of MFS (Habashi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: The aortopathy in the Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse model is not mediated by excessive TGF-β signaling and is exacerbated by loss of TGF-β signaling in smooth muscle cells.
source: Contradicting these results, others have shown that the aortopathy in the Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse model is not mediated by excessive TGF-β signaling and in fact is exacerbated by loss of TGF-β signaling in smooth muscle cells (Wei et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: TGF-β signaling protects against abdominal aortic aneurysms in angiotensin II-infused mice.
source: Furthermore, TGF-β signaling protects against abdominal aortic aneurysms in angiotensin II-infused mice (Angelov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: LDS is caused by pathogenic mutations in TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD2, SMAD3, TGFB2, and TGFB3.
source: Furthermore, the related syndrome LDS is caused by pathogenic mutations in several different components of the TGF-β pathway, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD2, SMAD3, and the ligands, TGFB2 and TGFB3.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: LDS mutations all cause missense amino acid substitutions that have been either verified in vitro, or are predicted to be loss of function.
source: These mutations all cause missense amino acid substitutions that have been either verified in vitro, or are predicted to be loss of function, implying that LDS is caused by attenuated TGF-β signaling (Horbelt et al., 2010; Cardoso et al., 2012; Schepers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Histological and biochemical studies of aortic tissue derived from LDS patients reveal an apparent high TGF-β signaling signature.
source: However, paradoxically, histological and biochemical studies of aortic tissue derived from LDS patients reveal an apparent high TGF-β signaling signature (van de Laar et al., 2012; Gallo et al., 2014; Lindsay et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Both SMAD-mediated and non-SMAD-mediated TGF-β signaling has been reported to be increased in primary dermal fibroblasts from SGS patients.
source: SGS is caused by mutations in SKI, and both SMAD-mediated and non-SMAD-mediated TGF-β signaling has been reported to be increased in primary dermal fibroblasts from SGS patients (Doyle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: SKI and SKIL play important roles in proliferation, differentiation, transformation, and tumor progression.
source: The co-repressors SKI and SKIL play important roles in a number of different cellular processes including proliferation, differentiation, transformation, and tumor progression (Bonnon and Atanasoski, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to review literature.

claim: SKI and SKIL are dimeric proteins that interact with both phosphorylated SMAD2 and SMAD3 via short motifs at their N-termini.
source: They are dimeric proteins that interact with both phosphorylated SMAD2 and SMAD3 (PSMAD2 or PSMAD3) via short motifs at their N-termini, and with SMAD4 via a SAND domain (named after Sp100, AIRE-1, NucP41/75, DEAF-1) in the middle of both proteins (Deheuninck and Luo, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SKI and SKIL interact with SMAD4 via a SAND domain in the middle of both proteins.
source: They are dimeric proteins that interact with both phosphorylated SMAD2 and SMAD3 (PSMAD2 or PSMAD3) via short motifs at their N-termini, and with SMAD4 via a SAND domain (named after Sp100, AIRE-1, NucP41/75, DEAF-1) in the middle of both proteins (Deheuninck and Luo, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The Dachshund homology domain (DHD) in SKI and SKIL is thought to be important for R-SMAD binding.
source: Between these two domains lies a Dachshund homology domain (DHD), which is thought to also be important for R-SMAD binding (Wilson et al., 2004; Ueki and Hayman, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SKI and SKIL contain a leucine zipper domain in their C-termini, through which they dimerize.
source: SKI and SKIL both contain a leucine zipper domain in their C-termini, through which they dimerize (Deheuninck and Luo, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SKI and SKIL bind with SMAD4 to SMAD binding elements (SBEs) of TGF-β/Activin target genes, and recruit co-repressors such as NCOR1 or SIN3A.
source: In one model, SKI and SKIL bind with SMAD4 to SMAD binding elements (SBEs) of TGF-β/Activin target genes, and recruit co-repressors such as NCOR1 or SIN3A (Tokitou et al., 1999; Nomura et al., 1999; Stroschein et al., 1999; Deheuninck and Luo, 2009).
evidence: This is one proposed mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Upon TGF-β/Activin signaling, SKI and SKIL are rapidly degraded by the E3 ubiquitin ligase, RNF111, a process that requires SKI/SKIL binding to PSMAD2 or PSMAD3.
source: Upon TGF-β/Activin signaling, SKI and SKIL are rapidly degraded by the E3 ubiquitin ligase, RNF111 (formerly known as Arkadia), a process that requires SKI/SKIL binding to PSMAD2 or PSMAD3 (Le Scolan et al., 2008; Levy et al., 2007; Nagano et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Degradation of SKI and SKIL allows activated SMAD3–SMAD4 complexes to bind the exposed SBEs and activate target gene transcription.
source: This then allows the activated SMAD3–SMAD4 complexes to bind the exposed SBEs and activate target gene transcription (Levy et al., 2007; Stroschein et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The heterozygous missense mutations that cause SGS have been mapped in SKI to the N-terminal R-SMAD-binding domain, with some small deletions and point mutations also found in the DHD.
source: The heterozygous missense mutations that cause SGS have been mapped in SKI to the N-terminal R-SMAD-binding domain, with some small deletions and point mutations also found in the DHD, which is also necessary for R-SMAD binding (Carmignac et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012; Schepers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of SMAD4 in HEK293T and HaCaT cells abolished ligand-induced SKI/SKIL degradation.
source: Deletion of SMAD4 in multiple clones of both cell types abolished ligand-induced SKI/SKIL degradation (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 1A and 1B showing SKI/SKIL levels remain unchanged after TGF-β/Activin treatment in SMAD4 knockout cells.

claim: Knockout of SMAD2 or SMAD3 individually or together abolished TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI and SKIL.
source: By knocking out SMAD2 or SMAD3 individually or together, we also confirmed that these R-SMADs are absolutely required for TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI and SKIL and act redundantly (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 1C showing SKI/SKIL levels remain unchanged after Activin treatment in SMAD2/SMAD3 knockout cells.

claim: SMAD2 and SMAD3 act redundantly in TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI and SKIL.
source: By knocking out SMAD2 or SMAD3 individually or together, we also confirmed that these R-SMADs are absolutely required for TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI and SKIL and act redundantly (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that knockout of either SMAD2 or SMAD3 alone is sufficient to block SKI/SKIL degradation.

claim: R-SMADs and SMAD4 are all essential for TGF-β/Activin-dependent SKI/SKIL degradation.
source: Thus, R-SMADs and SMAD4 are all essential for TGF-β/Activin-dependent SKI/SKIL degradation.
evidence: This is concluded from the knockout experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Amino acids 11–45 of SKI are sufficient for binding to PSMAD2 and PSMAD3 upon TGF-β stimulation.
source: This revealed that amino acids 11–45 of SKI are sufficient for binding to PSMAD2 and PSMAD3 upon TGF-β stimulation, whilst the unphosphorylated SMADs did not bind to any of the SKI peptides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide pulldown assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Unphosphorylated SMADs do not bind to SKI peptides.
source: This revealed that amino acids 11–45 of SKI are sufficient for binding to PSMAD2 and PSMAD3 upon TGF-β stimulation, whilst the unphosphorylated SMADs did not bind to any of the SKI peptides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide pulldown assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Six different SGS mutations in the SKI peptide 11–45 prevented binding of PSMAD2 and PSMAD3.
source: To determine the effect of these mutations on R-SMAD interaction, we introduced six different SGS mutations into the SKI peptide 11–45 and showed that they all prevented binding of PSMAD2 and PSMAD3, and as a result, also SMAD4 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide pulldown assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SGS mutations in SKIL (equivalent to those in SKI) prevented binding of PSMAD2 and PSMAD3.
source: These results were also confirmed with the equivalent mutations in SKIL (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide pulldown assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The interaction of SKI with SMAD2 is mediated via the SMAD2 MH2 domain.
source: We proved that the interaction with SMAD2 was mediated via its MH2 domain using a mouse embryonic fibroblast cell line that expresses a truncated SMAD2 protein comprising just the MH2 domain (Piek et al., 2001; Das et al., 2009; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide pulldown assays shown in Figure 4C and 4D using SMAD2 MH2 domain.

claim: Eight residues in SKI (Thr20, Leu21, Phe24, Ser28, Ser31, Leu32, Gly34, and Pro35) are intolerant to almost any amino acid substitution for PSMAD3–SMAD4 binding.
source: Eight residues are intolerant to almost any amino acid substitution (Thr20, Leu21, Phe24, Ser28, Ser31, Leu32, Gly34, and Pro35).
evidence: This is determined from the peptide array shown in Figure 4E and quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Six of the eight crucial residues for R-SMAD binding (Leu21, Ser28, Ser31, Leu32, Gly34, and Pro35) are amino acids known to be mutated in SGS patients.
source: Strikingly, six of these residues are the amino acids known to be mutated in SGS patients, and the array results readily explain why these residues are mutated to a number of different amino acids in SGS (Figure 4E; for quantification, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the peptide array data in Figure 4E showing these residues are critical for binding.

claim: The crystal structure of the SKI peptide with the phosphorylated SMAD2 MH2 domain was determined at 2 Å resolution.
source: The structure was determined by molecular replacement and refined at 2 Å resolution and readily explained why the crucial amino acids identified in the peptide were required for SMAD2 binding (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The dissociation constant (Kd) of the SKI peptide to the SMAD2 MH2 domain trimer is in the low nanomolar range.
source: Analysis of the binding affinity of the SKI peptide to the SMAD2 MH2 domain trimer indicated that the dissociation constant (Kd) was in the low nanomolar range (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by biolayer interferometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The SKI peptide binds on the outside face of the SMAD2 MH2 domain at the three helix bundle, comprising helices 3, 4, and 5.
source: The SKI peptide binds on the outside face of the MH2 domain at the so-called three helix bundle, comprising helices 3, 4, and 5 (Wu et al., 2001; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 5A.

claim: SKI can only bind SMAD2 in its phosphorylated trimeric state.
source: Thus, SKI can only bind SMAD2 in its phosphorylated trimeric state.
evidence: This is concluded from structural comparison shown in Figure 5G and 5H, demonstrating that Trp448 is in the correct orientation for SKI binding only in the trimeric state.

claim: In three independent clonal cell lines carrying the P35S SKI mutation, the binding to endogenous phosphorylated SMAD2 was severely compromised, compared with WT SKI.
source: In three independent clonal cell lines carrying the P35S SKI mutation, the binding to endogenous phosphorylated SMAD2 was severely compromised, compared with WT SKI (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The binding of P35S SKI to SMAD4 was unchanged compared to WT SKI.
source: The binding to SMAD4, however, was unchanged in the mutant cell lines, as the SGS mutations do not affect the SKI SAND domain, which is responsible for SMAD4 binding (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: P35S SKI levels remained stable after Activin treatment, whilst WT SKI protein is almost entirely degraded after 1 hr of Activin treatment.
source: At both time points, we clearly demonstrated that P35S SKI levels remained stable, whilst in the parental cell lines, SKI protein is almost entirely degraded after 1 hr of Activin treatment (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The presence of mutated SKI had no effect on the Activin-induced degradation of SKIL.
source: The presence of mutated SKI had no effect on the Activin-induced degradation of SKIL in these lines (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The P35S mutation renders SKI completely resistant to ligand-induced degradation.
source: Thus, the P35S mutation renders SKI completely resistant to ligand-induced degradation.
evidence: This is concluded from the Western blot data in Figure 6B.

claim: After Activin stimulation, the binding of WT SKI to SBEs is lost, whilst the binding of P35S SKI is retained.
source: Consistent with our prediction, both WT and P35S SKI bound the SBEs with SMAD4 in the absence of signal, but after Activin stimulation, the binding of WT SKI is lost, whilst the binding of P35S SKI is retained (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA pulldown assay shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There was a significant reduction in Activin-induced CAGA12-Luciferase activity in the P35S SKI cells compared to the parental cell line.
source: Strikingly, we found a significant reduction in Activin-induced CAGA12-Luciferase activity in the P35S SKI cells compared to the parental cell line (Figure 6D), while BMP4-induced BRE-Luciferase activity was similar in all cell lines (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: BMP4-induced BRE-Luciferase activity was similar in P35S SKI cells and parental cells.
source: Strikingly, we found a significant reduction in Activin-induced CAGA12-Luciferase activity in the P35S SKI cells compared to the parental cell line (Figure 6D), while BMP4-induced BRE-Luciferase activity was similar in all cell lines (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: SGS mutations in SKI lead to inhibition of TGF-β/Activin-induced transcription mediated by PSMAD3–SMAD4 complexes.
source: The results indicate that SGS mutations in SKI lead to inhibition of TGF-β/Activin-induced transcription mediated by PSMAD3–SMAD4 complexes.
evidence: This is concluded from the luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 6D.

claim: In control fibroblasts, SKI expression is abrogated upon TGF-β stimulation after 1 hr, while in the SGS-derived fibroblasts, SKI protein remains relatively stable.
source: Indeed, in control fibroblasts, SKI expression is abrogated upon TGF-β stimulation after 1 hr, while in the SGS-derived fibroblasts, SKI protein remains relatively stable (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Of the 339 genes that were differentially expressed in normal fibroblasts after 1 hr of TGF-β treatment, 60% (202 genes) were induced or repressed less efficiently in the L32V mutant fibroblasts.
source: We found that of the 339 genes that were differentially expressed in normal fibroblasts after 1 hr of TGF-β treatment, 60% (202 genes) were induced or repressed less efficiently in the L32V mutant fibroblasts, and of these, 97 genes were not significantly differentially expressed in the mutant cells at all (Figure 7—source data 1, Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Of the 339 genes differentially expressed in normal fibroblasts after 1 hr of TGF-β treatment, 97 genes were not significantly differentially expressed in the L32V mutant cells.
source: We found that of the 339 genes that were differentially expressed in normal fibroblasts after 1 hr of TGF-β treatment, 60% (202 genes) were induced or repressed less efficiently in the L32V mutant fibroblasts, and of these, 97 genes were not significantly differentially expressed in the mutant cells at all (Figure 7—source data 1, Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: After an 8 hr TGF-β induction, 4769 genes were differentially expressed in the normal fibroblasts, and of these 75% (3556 genes) were induced or repressed less efficiently in the L32V mutant cells.
source: After an 8 hr TGF-β induction, we found that 4769 genes were differentially expressed in the normal fibroblasts, and of these 75% (3556 genes) were induced or repressed less efficiently in the L32V mutant cells, and 880 genes were not significantly differentially expressed in the mutant cells at all (Figure 7—source data 1, Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: After an 8 hr TGF-β induction, 880 genes were not significantly differentially expressed in the L32V mutant cells.
source: After an 8 hr TGF-β induction, we found that 4769 genes were differentially expressed in the normal fibroblasts, and of these 75% (3556 genes) were induced or repressed less efficiently in the L32V mutant cells, and 880 genes were not significantly differentially expressed in the mutant cells at all (Figure 7—source data 1, Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: The presence of SGS point mutations in SKI that render it resistant to ligand-induced degradation result in attenuated TGF-β responses for a substantial subset of target genes.
source: Thus, we conclude that the presence of SGS point mutations in SKI that render it resistant to ligand-induced degradation, result in attenuated TGF-β responses for a substantial subset of target genes.
evidence: This is concluded from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B, C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: In unstimulated cells, SKI and SKIL interact with the E3 ubiquitin ligase, RNF111, although this binding per se does not lead to SKI/SKIL degradation.
source: We and others have also shown that in unstimulated cells, SKI and SKIL interact with the E3 ubiquitin ligase, RNF111, although this binding per se does not lead to SKI/SKIL degradation (Le Scolan et al., 2008; Levy et al., 2007; Nagano et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An intact functional phosphorylated R-SMAD–SMAD4 trimer is required to bind to SKIL to induce its ligand-dependent degradation.
source: Second, we clearly demonstrate for the first time that an intact functional phosphorylated R-SMAD–SMAD4 trimer is required to bind to SKIL to induce its ligand-dependent degradation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SMAD4 mutant rescue experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: SMAD4 mutants that cannot form a canonical activated R-SMAD–SMAD4 trimer cannot rescue ligand-induced SKIL degradation.
source: Critically, we show that SMAD4 mutants that cannot form a canonical activated R-SMAD–SMAD4 trimer cannot rescue ligand-induced SKIL degradation, neither can SMAD4 mutants that do not interact with the SAND domain of SKIL.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: SMAD4 mutants that do not interact with the SAND domain of SKIL cannot rescue ligand-induced SKIL degradation.
source: Critically, we show that SMAD4 mutants that cannot form a canonical activated R-SMAD–SMAD4 trimer cannot rescue ligand-induced SKIL degradation, neither can SMAD4 mutants that do not interact with the SAND domain of SKIL.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: TGF-β/Activin-induced SKIL degradation occurs only when SKIL interacts simultaneously with phosphorylated R-SMADs and with SMAD4, which in turn must interact with each other in a transcriptionally active trimer.
source: Thus, we conclude that TGF-β/Activin-induced SKIL degradation occurs only when SKIL interacts simultaneously with phosphorylated R-SMADs and with SMAD4, which in turn must interact with each other in a transcriptionally active trimer.
evidence: This is concluded from the SMAD4 mutant rescue experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: SKIL binding to the R-SMAD–SMAD4 complex does not disrupt it.
source: This strongly indicates that SKIL binding to the R-SMAD–SMAD4 complex does not disrupt it.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for an intact R-SMAD–SMAD4 complex for SKIL degradation.

claim: The crystal structure of the SAND domain of SKIL with the SMAD4 MH2 domain revealed that SKIL interacts with SMAD4 in two states: an 'open' and a 'closed' conformation.
source: This structure revealed that SKIL interacts with SMAD4 in two states: an 'open' and a 'closed' conformation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walldén et al., 2017.

claim: In the open conformation, SKIL can bind the R-SMAD–SMAD4 complex without intermolecular clashes or further structural readjustment.
source: In the open conformation, the authors showed that SKIL can bind the R-SMAD–SMAD4 complex without intermolecular clashes or further structural readjustment, whereas in the closed state, structural reorganization within the SMAD heterotrimer is required to allow binding of SKIL, as has been observed in the previous structure of SKI with SMAD4 (Wu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walldén et al., 2017.

claim: The open conformation is the biologically and functionally relevant mode of SKIL-SMAD4 binding.
source: Furthermore, surface plasmon resonance indicated only one dominant binding mode for SKIL and SMAD4, leading to the conclusion that the open conformation is the biologically and functionally relevant mode and that the closed conformation may be the result of crystal packing forces (Walldén et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walldén et al., 2017.

claim: The residues that allow the binding in the open conformation are highly conserved between SKI and SKIL.
source: Note that the residues that allow the binding in the open conformation are highly conserved between SKI and SKIL, suggesting that both repressors bind to an intact activated R-SMAD–SMAD4 complex, which is required for their degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence conservation and structural data.

claim: Patients with 1p36 deletion syndrome, who are haploinsufficient for SKI, do not have SGS.
source: Finally, our finding that SGS mutations in SKI lead to its stabilization and are not equivalent to loss of SKI function also explains why patients with 1p36 deletion syndrome, who are haploinsufficient for SKI, do not have SGS.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Colmenares et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2013.

claim: Many of the same organs are affected in both 1p36 deletion syndrome and SGS.
source: However, unsurprisingly, many of the same organs are affected in both syndromes (Colmenares et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: A PSMAD2/3–SMAD4 ternary complex is essential for TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI/SKIL.
source: A PSMAD2/3–SMAD4 ternary complex is essential for TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI/SKIL
evidence: This is the title of a results section and is demonstrated by the experiments in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: The D351H and D537Y SMAD4 mutants lost their ability to bind SMAD2 upon TGF-β induction, but retained the interaction with SKIL.
source: As predicted, the D351H and D537Y SMAD4 mutants had lost their ability to bind SMAD2 upon TGF-β induction, but retained the interaction with SKIL.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The A433E and I435Y SMAD4 mutants were unable to bind SKIL, but could interact with SMAD2 upon TGF-β stimulation.
source: By contrast, A433E and I435Y SMAD4 mutants were unable to bind SKIL, but could interact with SMAD2 upon TGF-β stimulation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The D351H and D537Y SMAD4 mutants failed to rescue the ability of TGF-β to induce expression of CAGA12-Luciferase in HaCaT SMAD4-null cells.
source: Furthermore, as expected, D351H and D537Y SMAD4 mutants failed to rescue the ability of TGF-β to induce expression of CAGA12-Luciferase in HaCaT SMAD4-null cells or rescue TGF-β-induced transcription of target genes, but the A433E and I435Y SMAD4 mutants rescued these responses almost as well as WT SMAD4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The A433E and I435Y SMAD4 mutants rescued TGF-β-induced transcription of target genes almost as well as WT SMAD4.
source: Furthermore, as expected, D351H and D537Y SMAD4 mutants failed to rescue the ability of TGF-β to induce expression of CAGA12-Luciferase in HaCaT SMAD4-null cells or rescue TGF-β-induced transcription of target genes, but the A433E and I435Y SMAD4 mutants rescued these responses almost as well as WT SMAD4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assay and qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Reintroduction of WT SMAD4 in SMAD4-null cells caused a 50% reduction in SKIL levels in TGF-β-induced cells compared to those treated with SB-431542.
source: In a Western blot assay using nuclear extract, we found that reintroduction of WT SMAD4 in SMAD4-null cells caused a 50% reduction in SKIL levels in TGF-β-induced cells compared to those treated with SB-431542 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: None of the four SMAD4 mutants (D351H, D537Y, A433E, I435Y) could rescue TGF-β-induced SKIL degradation.
source: However, none of the four SMAD4 mutants could rescue TGF-β-induced SKIL degradation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot, flow cytometry, and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 2B, 2C, and 3.

claim: Treatment with TGF-β for 1 hr caused a 52% reduction in the relative median fluorescence intensity in the EGFP-SMAD4 WT-expressing cells, reflecting SKIL levels, compared to cells treated with SB-431542.
source: Treatment with TGF-β for 1 hr caused a 52% reduction in the relative median fluorescence intensity in the EGFP-SMAD4 WT-expressing cells, reflecting SKIL levels, compared to cells treated with SB-431542 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: For all four SMAD4 mutants tested, the median fluorescence was not decreased by TGF-β treatment.
source: However, for all four SMAD4 mutants tested, the median fluorescence was not decreased by TGF-β treatment (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Within a canonical activated ternary SMAD complex, the R-SMAD component binds to the N-terminal region of SKIL/SKI, whilst SMAD4 binds the SAND domain, and both interactions are absolutely required for SKIL/SKI degradation.
source: This suggests that within a canonical activated ternary SMAD complex, the R-SMAD component binds to the N-terminal region of SKIL/SKI, whilst SMAD4 binds the SAND domain, and both interactions are absolutely required for SKIL/SKI degradation.
evidence: This is concluded from the SMAD4 mutant rescue experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The SGS mutations discovered so far mostly cluster within the 11–45 region of SKI.
source: The SGS mutations discovered so far mostly cluster within this 11–45 region of SKI and a few deletions and point mutations have additionally been mapped in the DHD domain (Carmignac et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012; Schepers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The residues mutated in SGS are completely conserved, both between species, and also in the related protein, SKIL.
source: The residues mutated are completely conserved, both between species, and also in the related protein, SKIL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Carmignac et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Thr20 and Phe24 are crucial residues for binding the PSMAD3–SMAD4 complex, but have not yet been reported as disease mutations.
source: In addition, Thr20 and Phe24 are also crucial residues for binding the PSMAD3–SMAD4 complex, but have not yet been reported as disease mutations.
evidence: This is determined from the peptide array shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mutations in nine amino acids (between positions 19-35 in SKI) do not impair the binding to PSMAD3–SMAD4, and almost any other amino acid apart from proline can be tolerated at these positions.
source: Mutations in the other nine amino acids do not impair the binding, and almost any other amino acid apart from proline can be tolerated at these positions.
evidence: This is determined from the peptide array shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The phosphorylated SMAD2 MH2 domain is trimeric in solution.
source: We confirmed using SEC-MALLS that the phosphorylated SMAD2 MH2 domain was indeed trimeric in solution (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The N-terminal helix of SKI packs against helix 3 of SMAD2.
source: The N-terminal helix of SKI packs against helix 3 of SMAD2, and the C-terminal portion of the SKI peptide, which contains the critical Gly34 and Pro35, forms a sharp turn that is stabilized by pi-stacking coordination between Phe24 of SKI, Trp448 of SMAD2, and Pro35 of SKI (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 5B.

claim: The C-terminal portion of the SKI peptide forms a sharp turn that is stabilized by pi-stacking coordination between Phe24 of SKI, Trp448 of SMAD2, and Pro35 of SKI.
source: The N-terminal helix of SKI packs against helix 3 of SMAD2, and the C-terminal portion of the SKI peptide, which contains the critical Gly34 and Pro35, forms a sharp turn that is stabilized by pi-stacking coordination between Phe24 of SKI, Trp448 of SMAD2, and Pro35 of SKI (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 5B.

claim: The main chain carbonyl of Ser31 forms a hydrogen bond to the ND1 of Asn387 in helix 3 of SMAD2.
source: Other key interactions involving amino acids identified above as crucial for binding include the main chain carbonyl of Ser31, which forms a hydrogen bond to the ND1 of Asn387 in helix 3 (Figure 5C), and the hydroxyl group of SKI Thr20, which forms a hydrogen bond with the Gln455 at the end of helix 5 of SMAD2, and is nearly completely buried in the interface (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 5C.

claim: The hydroxyl group of SKI Thr20 forms a hydrogen bond with the Gln455 at the end of helix 5 of SMAD2, and is nearly completely buried in the interface.
source: Other key interactions involving amino acids identified above as crucial for binding include the main chain carbonyl of Ser31, which forms a hydrogen bond to the ND1 of Asn387 in helix 3 (Figure 5C), and the hydroxyl group of SKI Thr20, which forms a hydrogen bond with the Gln455 at the end of helix 5 of SMAD2, and is nearly completely buried in the interface (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 5D.

claim: The two leucine residues (Leu21 and Leu32) that are mutated in SGS are both buried in the structure.
source: The two leucine residues (Leu21 and Leu32) that are mutated in SGS are both buried in the structure (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: In the unphosphorylated SMAD2 structure, Tyr268 in the β1' strand is locked in a stable conformation in a hydrophobic pocket.
source: It was clear that in the unphosphorylated SMAD2 structure, Tyr268 in the so-called β1' strand (amino acids 261–274) is locked in a stable conformation in a hydrophobic pocket, and also forms a number of hydrogen bonds (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown by comparison with the structure of unphosphorylated SMAD2 MH2 domain in Figure 5G.

claim: In the unphosphorylated SMAD2 structure, the conformation of Tyr268 forces Trp448 into flattened orientation, which is incompatible with SKI binding.
source: Crucially, this conformation forces Trp448 into flattened orientation, which is incompatible with SKI binding through the pi-stacking involving SKI Phe24, SMAD2 Trp448, and SKI Pro35 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown by comparison with the structure of unphosphorylated SMAD2 MH2 domain in Figure 5G.

claim: MH2 domain trimerization generates a new binding site for the β1' strand on the adjacent MH2 domain subunit.
source: MH2 domain trimerization generates a new binding site for the β1' strand on the adjacent MH2 domain subunit (Figure 5H; Video 1).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 5H and Video 1.

claim: In the SMAD2 trimer, the hydroxy group of Tyr268 makes hydrogen bond contact with the carbonyl group of Asp450 and the main chain of Lys451 on the adjacent MH2 domain subunit.
source: In the trimer, the hydroxy group of Tyr268 makes hydrogen bond contact with the carbonyl group of Asp450 and the main chain of Lys451 on the adjacent MH2 domain subunit.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 5H.

claim: As a consequence of trimerization, Trp448 moves into an upright position in the trimer, allowing engagement with SKI.
source: As a consequence, Trp448 moves into an upright position in the trimer, allowing engagement with SKI.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 5H and Video 1.

claim: The G103V mutation in SKIL (corresponding to the SGS mutation G34V in SKI) led to reduction of SMAD2 binding in parental cells.
source: Transfection of G103V SKIL in HEK293T cells led to reduction of SMAD2 binding in parental cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The residual binding of G103V SKIL to SMAD2 was mediated via SMAD2's interaction with SMAD4, as it was lost in the SMAD4 knockout cells.
source: The residual binding was mediated via SMAD2's interaction with SMAD4, as it was lost in the SMAD4 knockout cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The SGS mutation in SKIL (G103V) led to resistance to Activin-induced degradation.
source: As observed above for SKI, the SGS mutation in SKIL led to resistance to Activin-induced degradation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), indicating that the R-SMAD interaction was essential.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A version of SKIL with mutations in the SAND domain (R314A, T315A, H317A, and W318E) was unable to interact with SMAD4 and was not degraded upon Activin stimulation.
source: In addition, we made a version of SKIL with mutations in the SAND domain (R314A, T315A, H317A, and W318E) that rendered it unable to interact with SMAD4 (referred to as SKIL ΔS4). This mutant was also not degraded upon Activin stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating an essential requirement for SMAD4 binding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and 1C.
